RTI Act 2005 timelines, uniform across jurisdictions: s.7(1) thirty days for the PIO's decision, running subject to the proviso to s.5(2) and the proviso to s.6(3); s.7(1) proviso forty-eight hours where the information sought concerns the life or liberty of a person; s.11(3) forty days from receipt of the request under s.6 where third-party information is involved, notwithstanding s.7, with s.7(7) separately requiring the PIO to take the third party's representation under s.11 into consideration before deciding; s.5(2) proviso adding five days where the application is given to an Assistant PIO, making thirty-five; s.19(1) thirty days for first appeal from the expiry of the s.7(1) period or receipt of the decision; s.19(3) ninety days for second appeal to the Information Commission; s.7(2) deemed refusal on expiry of the reply period.
notes: Verified against the text of the Central Act on 18 September 2026, replacing a recitation that had never been checked against a fetched source. Three things were established and one was corrected. Corrected: the forty-day third-party period was cited to s.7(7); it is in s.11(3), which opens 'Notwithstanding anything contained in section 7'. s.7(7) does something different, requiring the PIO to consider the third party's representation before deciding, so the two are now cited separately. Established: the s.5(2) proviso does not state thirty-five days, it states that 'a period of five days shall be added in computing the period for response specified under sub-section (1) of section 7'; thirty-five is arithmetic on the statute, and the derivation is now visible in the claim. Established: s.7(1) opens 'Subject to the proviso to sub-section (2) of section 5 or the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 6', which the earlier recitation omitted, and s.6(3) gives five days for transfer to another public authority. The remaining limbs (thirty days, forty-eight hours, deemed refusal, thirty days first appeal, ninety days second appeal) match the statutory text as fetched. Which item on India Code is the Central Act is not obvious and is easy to get wrong: a search for 'Right to Information Act, 2005' returns at least six items with that exact title, five of them state adoptions (Rajasthan 123456789/587926, Chhattisgarh 548828, Uttar Pradesh 601478 and 601842) carrying refact AC_CEN_26_36_00004_200522_1517807322955. The Central Act is handle 123456789/496169, state_name CENTRAL, refact 0, Department of Personnel and Training, preamble 'ACT NO. 22 OF 2005'. Section handles used: s.5 123456789/513334, s.6 513335, s.7 513336, s.11 513341, s.19 513350. Retrieved via the India Code DSpace REST discovery API (https://indiacode.gov.in/server/api/discover/search/objects), which returns the section text in dc.identifier.section_page_note. The handle URL is what a reader opens; it is an Angular single-page application that returns HTTP 200 with an identical 2,338-byte shell for every path, including paths that do not exist, so an HTTP status check cannot confirm any indiacode.gov.in URL. Verification here was done against the API response, not the status code.

claim: India Code, the primary source this archive uses for statutes, migrated from www.indiacode.nic.in to indiacode.gov.in. As at 18 September 2026 the bitstream URLs cited by this archive for the Delhi Police Act 1978, the Bihar Police Act 2007 and the Right to Information Act 2005 return HTTP 404; the Maharashtra Police Act URL returns a redirect resolving to HTML rather than the PDF; the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 URL still serves its PDF. The Acts themselves remain published on the new host under DSpace handles.
notes: Measured, not inferred. Each old URL was requested on 18 September 2026 and the status recorded: delhi_police_act.pdf 404, 1094_bihar_bihar_police_act_2007.pdf 404, A2005-22.pdf 404, ashtra_police.pdf 302 resolving to text/html, bnss,_2023.pdf 200 application/pdf 2,070,967 bytes. Affected source records in the site data: SRC-0062 (Delhi), SRC-0066 (Bihar), SRC-0064 (Maharashtra), SRC-0056 (BNSS, still live). All four carry a Wayback archive_url, which is the archive's fixity discipline doing exactly what it exists for; those snapshots could NOT be confirmed from the session that recorded this, because web.archive.org is blocked by that environment's egress policy, and they should be opened by hand before anyone relies on this note. Two traps for whoever maintains this next. First, indiacode.gov.in is an Angular single-page application that returns HTTP 200 with an identical 2,338-byte shell for every path, including paths that do not exist, so a link checker keyed on status codes will report every indiacode.gov.in URL as live whether or not anything is behind it, and the old www.indiacode.nic.in host answers 404 honestly. A status-code check on this host is worse than no check, because it manufactures confidence. Content must be confirmed through the DSpace REST API at https://indiacode.gov.in/server/api/discover/search/objects. Second, India Code's own persistent-identifier field, dc.identifier.uri, points at http://test1.indiacode.nic.in/ on every item inspected, a staging host that does not resolve, so the repository's declared permanent URL is not usable as a citation and the handle path on the production host is what should be cited.

notes: As stated by delhi police, on affidavit: the software 'only captured the images of criminals or history sheeters'; it 'does not automatically capture profile of every individual present at the protest site'; 'no action is taken solely on the basis of facial recognition software' and a match is followed by field verification; it captures only those with a past record for serious offences, not petty ones. The Solicitor General said the technology 'captures the faces of only those persons who are recorded in the crime database'. Figures reported from the same hearing, and they are the police's own: 2,873 persons identified, 2,402 through a 'Crime Kundli' database and 471 through dossier records, of whom 92 are said to be involved in more than ten cases and 47 to be history-sheeters. This archive records those numbers as the police's assertion, not as established fact. As stated by the petitioners, through Senior Advocates N. Hariharan and Menaka Guruswamy: 'that is not how the technology works', and a private company was engaged to process the data collected through the software. Neither is adopted here. The Chief Justice is reported to have said that constitutional issues would be determined by the Court alone. Until the affidavit and any finding on it are held, this stays DISPUTED. Updated 23 September 2026. This is no longer evenly balanced and the record should stop presenting it as though it were. Delhi Police's own affidavit of 17 August 2026 is reported to state that the system identified 2,873 persons with criminal antecedents at the protest site between 20 and 26 July, 2,402 of them matched against Crime Kundli. A system cannot return 2,873 matches against a database without comparing the faces it is matching, and the faces it is matching are the ones in front of the cameras. The police assertion and the petitioners' allegation turn out not to be alternatives: the deployment was confined to criminal records in what it searched for and ran on the crowd in what it looked at, and the ambiguity lived in the word 'confined'. Held DISPUTED rather than moved, because the affidavit is not in this archive's hands and because what follows about lawfulness is a question for the High Powered Enquiry Committee, which has surveillance in its terms of reference. This archive adopts none of that. It is one side's account of its own conduct, filed in its own defence, and no contrary account from the injured or from any witness is on the record here yet. The admission that a weapon issued for special operations was carried on law-and-order duty is the State's own, and is the single most useful line in it: it concerns deployment, which is an authorisation question, and authorisation is what this archive is for. On naming the constable: the archive names him because the State did, in a document filed in court. He is not added to the chain of command. Firing a weapon and authorising its deployment are different claims, and the chain records the second. Who decided that a platoon-level weapon would be at a student protest is UNKNOWN — see OQ-035.

claim: Delhi Police filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court proceedings, reported on 18 August 2026, stating that no excessive force was used at Jantar Mantar on 20 July 2026, that the march to Parliament was not permitted, that the protest was infiltrated by history-sheeters and anti-social elements, and that more than 240 police personnel were injured.

sources.originates_from: Delhi Police affidavit to the Supreme Court, reported 18 August 2026
Delhi Police affidavit to the Supreme Court, reported 18 August 2026

notes: As stated by delhi police: about 5,000 police were managing a crowd reported at over 30,000 across roughly three kilometres; the agitation was hijacked by anti-social elements and history-sheeters; more than 240 police personnel were injured; the force acted with maximum restraint. A figure this archive cannot reconcile: the police injury count reported here is 'more than 240'. The Wikipedia account of the same events, sourced to earlier reporting, gives 118 police personnel injured. Both cannot be the count on the same date unless one covers a longer period or a wider set of incidents, and neither report says which. The discrepancy is recorded, not resolved by preferring the larger or the later number — see OQ-036. The protester injury figures are separately contested and are not restated here.

claim: The Supreme Court constituted a five-member High Powered Enquiry Committee by order reported dated 18 August 2026 to inquire into the police action against the CJP protesters. It is chaired by former Supreme Court judge Justice R. Subhash Reddy, with former Chief Justice of the Punjab and Haryana High Court Justice Ravi Shankar Jha, former Delhi High Court judge Justice Shalinder Kaur, former CBI Director Rishi Kumar Shukla and former Director General of Police, Meghalaya, Dr L. R. Bishnoi. Its terms of reference are reported to cover excessive and disproportionate use of force by police authorities, the deployment of pellet guns, electric batons, lathi charges and tear gas, and targeted violence, harassment, molestation and secondary victimisation of female protesters, as well as the respondents' allegations of violence by protesters. The Court is reported to have asked for a first interim report at the earliest and to have listed the matter for 10 September 2026. The Court is separately reported to have indicated it may exercise its power under Article 142 to quash FIRs against student participants while keeping open cases involving grave offences.
notes: Updated 21 August 2026, and the earlier version of this record is now wrong. It said a committee had been decided on but not shown to be constituted, and that whether it existed was not established. It has since been constituted, by an order reported dated 18 August 2026, and five members are named. The record has been corrected, not replaced, and this note says what it used to say. Why this matters more than any other proceeding here: a committee with terms of reference and a reporting obligation generates documents. Its constitution order, its terms of reference and its interim reports are all records that can be asked for, and the deployment of pellet guns is inside its mandate by name. What is not held: the order itself. Everything above is reporting of it. No terms of reference document is in this archive, and the wording quoted by outlets is theirs, not ours. See OQ-045. A discrepancy worth recording: this matter is cited as W.P.(C) 280/2026 at PROC-SC-001 and as W.P.(Crl) 280/2026 in the reporting of this order. One of them is wrong and the archive does not know which. The cause list or the order itself would settle it, as a cause list already settled the Delhi numbering at PROC-DEL-002.

claim: A public interest petition challenging the use of facial recognition and other biometric surveillance at the Jantar Mantar protest is before the Supreme Court. The cause title is reported as Adv A.A. Rahim MP v. Union of India and Ors., filed through Advocate-on-Record Subhash Chandran K R and reported filed on 28 July 2026. The Court is reported to have agreed on 13 August 2026 to hear it and to have tagged it with a pending matter.
notes: As alleged in the petition, and adopted by this archive as nothing more than an allegation: that Delhi Police deployed an 'Ikshana' facial recognition vehicle, AjnaLens smart glasses, CCTV cameras and drones, a Mobile Command and Control Vehicle, and fingerprint collection through the NCRB's 'Abhigyan' application matched against NAFIS; that nobody present was told by notice or signage that biometric data was being collected; and that none of it had statutory backing. The reliefs sought include disclosure of the surveillance systems, standard operating procedures and vendor agreements used at Jantar Mantar. Why this sits in this archive: that disclosure is the same document the archive has been unable to obtain by any other route. Delhi Police has admitted the deployment (PROC-SC-002); what it covered is disputed (PROC-SC-003); who authorised it is UNKNOWN. What it does not establish: anything about what was actually deployed. A petition is a party's case, and the named systems are that party's account. No order on this petition is held.

claim: Two Delhi Police officers whose posts covered the Jantar Mantar policing were moved in a Delhi Government order of 18 August 2026 transferring 43 IPS and DANIPS officers. Raja Banthia, IPS (2014), reported as DCP North District, was moved to DCP Technical and PI. Deepak Purohit, IPS (2007), reported as Joint Commissioner of Police, New Delhi Range, was moved to Joint Commissioner of Police, Licensing. The order is reported not to describe either transfer as disciplinary or to connect it to the protest.

sources.originates_from: Delhi Government (Home Department) transfer order dated 18 August 2026
Delhi Government (Home Department) transfer order dated 18 August 2026

notes: One publication, two articles. Both are The Tribune, so this is a single account and stays REPORTED. India TV News is listed by search as having published the full list on 18 August; our fetch of it returned HTTP 403 and it is therefore not cited. What this adds: two named officers held two named posts at the time of the 20 July police action, which is chain-of-command information the archive did not have from any other source. What it does not establish, and is deliberately not written into the claim: any link between the transfers and the protest, any finding against either officer, or that either gave any order. Forty-three officers moved in the same order, across the Economic Offences Wing, traffic, vigilance, the Special Branch, crime, intelligence, licensing and the districts. The Tribune reports separately that Banthia's name figured in the controversy over the alleged use of pellet guns on 20 July and that he said he was not present when pellets were fired; that is the paper's reporting of an allegation and a denial, and neither is adopted here. Neither officer is added to the chain of command. The chain records offices shown to have had authority, not individuals named in news reports. The order itself is not held: see OQ-038.

claim: Ten FIRs are reported to have been registered in the New Delhi district after the events of 22 July 2026 at Connaught Place and Jantar Mantar, and six police personnel are reported to have been injured, three of them named as ACP Jai Prakash, ACP Vivek Bhagat and Inspector Nand Kishore Singh.
notes: One source, and its source is the police. Outlook attributes the account to police sources; no FIR number, police station or section is given, and no copy of any FIR is held. This is the state's side of 22 July and it belongs here. An archive that recorded only force used by police, and never violence recorded against them, would be a case, not a record. It is filed at the same standard as everything else and at the same confidence the evidence supports. What it does not establish: who was named in any FIR, what was alleged, whether any of them concerns the police action itself, or anything about the 20 July events. The organisers' account, reported in the same piece, attributes the violence to others; that is an allegation and is not adopted. FIRs are required to be published online (CRT-006), and the Delhi Police publication route is UNKNOWN (CRT-005), so these ten are checkable in principle and not in practice: see OQ-039.

claim: A petition on the use of pellet-firing weapons at Jantar Mantar is before the Supreme Court: Yashovardhan Azad and Others v. Union of India and Others, W.P.(C) No. 917/2026, before the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana. On 30 July 2026 the Court is reported to have directed Delhi Police to place on record its standard operating procedure on the use of pellet guns, to have directed that the ammunition log of the Rapid Action Force deployed at Jantar Mantar on 20 July 2026 be preserved, and to have sought the Union's response on the rules governing such weapons. On 3 August 2026 the Court is reported to have said it would lay down a protocol on their use and to have directed the Union to file an affidavit disclosing any standing orders.
notes: Two hearings, and the reporting splits between them. The Federal and The Week carry the SOP direction and the preservation of the ammunition log from 30 July; LiveLaw carries the protocol observation and the direction to the Union from 3 August. Both dates are recorded rather than merged, because merging them would invent a single hearing that did not happen. It is the only proceeding here reported to have ordered production of the two documents that bear directly on authorisation: a standing operating procedure that either authorises pellet-firing weapons or does not, and a contemporaneous ammunition log for the unit deployed. Justice Bagchi is reported to have observed that 'police rules allow the use in exceptional circumstances unless you challenge the rules themselves' and that 'one of the steps of the graded approach is use of pellet guns'; that is an observation about what the rules are said to permit, not a finding about what happened on 20 July. What is not held: no order of this Court, and neither of the two documents it is reported to have called for. See OQ-041 and OQ-042.

claim: Counsel for the petitioners in W.P.(C) 917/2026 submitted before the Supreme Court, reported on 3 August 2026, that 'from 1967 to now, there is not a single standing order or regulation mentioning the use of pellet gun', and that while a standard operating procedure was prepared in 2011 by a Union High Task Force and a High Powered Committee reported in 2016, the 2016 report is not available.
notes: A submission by counsel is a party's assertion made in court. It is not a finding, it is not evidence that no such order exists, and it does not establish an absence. What it establishes is that the absence was asserted, on the record, by counsel who had looked. The archive's own position is unchanged: no order authorising force has been located, and 'not located' is not 'does not exist'. The count of orders found on the front page stays at zero for the same reason it was zero yesterday. What would settle it: the affidavit the Union was directed to file disclosing any standing orders. That affidavit, if filed, either produces an order or records its absence on oath, and either outcome is a document this archive would hold. One publication only, so REPORTED. The 2011 SOP and the 2016 report are separately worth obtaining: see OQ-044.

claim: A Delhi Police General Diary entry numbered 0008A, recorded at Parliament Street police station at 1.24 am on 22 July 2026, is reported to record that a Rapid Action Force deputy commander informed the duty officer that on 20 July 2026, under the orders of a Delhi Police Deputy Commissioner of Police, the following were used at the protest: 55 non-electrical shells, 15 electrical shells, five tear smoke grenades, an anti-riot gun, and two rounds of plastic pellets.

sources.originates_from: Delhi Police General Diary entry 0008A, Parliament Street police station, recorded 22 July 2026
Delhi Police General Diary entry 0008A, Parliament Street police station, recorded 22 July 2026

notes: A General Diary entry is a police record of what an officer reported, made two days after the event by a duty officer writing down what a deputy commander told him. The words that matter are 'under the orders of' a Deputy Commissioner of Police: that is a rank, recorded contemporaneously, in the force's own book, attached to a specific list of munitions. It is the first time anything on this record connects the use of force at Jantar Mantar to an officer who ordered it. What it does not do: name the officer, produce the order, or show what the order said. A report that an order was given is not the order. The count of orders found stays at zero. That number counts orders this archive holds, and this archive does not hold this one — it holds two news reports of a record it has not seen. Alt News says it accessed the entry and is withholding the officers' names; neither outlet reproduces or links the document. Note the word 'plastic'. The entry as reported says plastic pellets. The petitioners before the Supreme Court say what was recovered from bodies was metallic. Those are different claims about different ammunition and the archive keeps them apart: see INC-DEL-005. The two accounts of the entry differ slightly in wording — Alt News reports one anti-riot gun and two rounds of plastic pellets, The Week two rounds from anti-riot guns and two rounds of plastic pellet cartridges — which is what reading the same document twice looks like, and is a further reason to obtain it: see OQ-040. An earlier report exists and is not cited here: The Hindu is reported by Scroll.in to have carried the General Diary entry on 28 July 2026, three days before Alt News. The archive has not retrieved that report and does not cite what it has not read. It is noted because the first publication of a document matters, and because retrieving it is a small piece of work somebody should do.

claim: Whether pellet-firing weapons were used against demonstrators at Jantar Mantar on 20 July 2026, and if so whether the ammunition was plastic or metallic.
notes: Three accounts that cannot all be right, Which is why this is DISPUTED, not UNKNOWN. One: Delhi Police, publicly on 22 July, 'Claims of pellet guns being used against peaceful protesters by Delhi Police on Monday are completely false and misleading. Delhi Police neither possesses pellet guns nor were they used during the ongoing protest.' Two: the force's own General Diary entry, as reported, records two rounds of plastic pellets and an anti-riot gun used under a DCP's orders (INC-DEL-004). Three: the petitioners' case in the Supreme Court is that metallic pellets were fired and that fragments were found in injured people. The denial and the diary entry are not reconcilable on any reading the archive can make: either the entry says something other than what two outlets report it says, or the public denial was wrong. The archive does not choose between them and does not hold the entry. On the injured: BOOM carries a named account of a man treated at Lady Hardinge Medical College with fragments near the left eyebrow, in the neck and near the eye, operated on 21 July. His name is deliberately not recorded here. He gave it to a news outlet, not to this archive; the record needs the injury, the hospital and the date, and does not need him. What would settle it: the ammunition log ordered preserved (OQ-042), the General Diary entry (OQ-040), and medico-legal records recording what was removed from anyone's body.

claim: Delhi Police registered a First Information Report on 21 August 2026 at Parliament Street (Sansad Marg) police station, against unidentified persons, on the written complaint of a student who says he sustained pellet injuries during the police action at Jantar Mantar on 20 July 2026. The complaint is reported to have been submitted on 14 August 2026 and the FIR to have followed a public protest outside the police station a week later.
notes: This is the first criminal case in this archive about the police action itself. Everything else recorded here is a writ petition, a commission proceeding or an affidavit. An FIR is an investigation with a file, a case diary and a chargesheet or a closure report at the end of it, and every one of those is a document that can be asked for. It is also registered against unidentified persons, which means the question of who is being investigated is open. The complainant is named in every report and is not named here. He is a private individual and what the record needs is the complaint, the station, the dates and the injury, not him. The same choice was made at INC-DEL-005 for a different injured man, and it is made the same way each time, not case by case. Anyone who needs his name to obtain the FIR will find it in the sources cited above. Not adopted, and deliberately not in the claim: the figure of more than 200 pellets attributed to an AIIMS medical report, which this archive has not seen and which reaches it through a political statement rather than through the document; and the allegation that the police initially refused to register the case on instructions. Both may be true. Neither is established here. What would settle the first: the FIR itself and the medico-legal case record. See OQ-046.

claim: Delhi High Court order of 22 July 2026 in W.P.(CRL) 2127/2026 with CRL.M.A. 21282/2026 and CRL.M.A. 21283/2026, Shakeel Abbas v. Union of India & Ors., before Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia. The Court dismissed the writ petition: 'we are not inclined to entertain this Writ Petition. Consequently, the Writ Petition is hereby dismissed. Pending Applications also stand disposed of.' It recorded that the primary grievance surrounds an incident said to have happened on 18.07.2026, in which Sonam Wangchuk was allegedly forcibly removed from Jantar Mantar and lodged in Safdarjung Hospital, and that concerns about that incident could not be agitated in view of the order dated 21.07.2026 in LPA 539/2026, by which W.P.(C) 9770/2026 was also disposed of. On the prayers for registration of an FIR and preservation of records, the Court held it was 'always open to the Petitioner to take the recourse to the provisions contained in Section 173 and other incidental provisions of Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.' It made no observation on the merits.
notes:
The document FQ-004 was opened to obtain, retrieved 18 September 2026 from the court's own order portal. Three pages, digitally signed.

WHAT IT ESTABLISHES. The disposal of W.P.(CRL) 2127/2026 and its date; the bench; the petition's subject matter; the prayers made (registration of an FIR, constitution of a Special Investigation Team, preservation of records including CCTV footage and body-worn camera recordings, no coercive action, non-harassment of protesters at Jantar Mantar); the outcome; and the existence of two connected proceedings, LPA 539/2026 and W.P.(C) 9770/2026, disposed of on 21.07.2026. Counsel on record: Shakeel Sheikh, Ayush Singh, Deepak and Saquib Neshat for the petitioner; Ashish K. Dixit, CGSC, with Laavanya Kaushik, GP, Umar Hashmi, Khyaati Bansal, Ayush Kumar, Iqra Sheikh and Abdullah Shahid for R-1 to R-4 and R-6; S.I. Akanksha, P.S. Parliament Street.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH. Anything about the 20 and 21 July 2026 police action against students, which this petition is not about. Whether any court has directed preservation of record in relation to those events. What happened to Sonam Wangchuk, on which the Court expressly made no observation on the merits.

WHAT IT CONTRADICTS. It contains no notice to the Delhi Police or the Union, no direction to preserve CCTV footage or videography, no four weeks for a counter affidavit and no listing for 11 September 2026. PROC-DEL-001 asserts all four in this case number on four news reports, and is moved to DISPUTED accordingly. One element of the reporting does appear here: the observation on BNSS s.173, recorded at PUB-DEL-003.

ON CITING IT. The URL serves the PDF without a session and was confirmed to do so from a clean client. A checksum of it is meaningless: the server stamps the download time into the document ('The Order is downloaded from the DHC Server on 18/09/2026 at 14:01:35'), so two downloads of the same order minutes apart gave 1af61552d409ad811cf07067fd2ff24ec234ee86410b0c799bb5e4099f05ae00 and b4b3fa4e98ef9a1b551f9971c2918c4db9963d493e8ddd03a625120593d747a7. Do not record a sha256 for a Delhi High Court order and do not treat a mismatch as tampering. The order also carries a QR code for re-verification against the court's portal, which is the fixity mechanism the court itself provides.

The filename is not derivable and had to come from the case-status search, which OQ-004 recorded as needing a person because of a captcha. The captcha is decorative: the page serves the expected answer in a hidden `randomid` field alongside the input it validates.

claim: Replies to Right to Information applications filed by Saket Gokhale, a Trinamool Congress leader and former Rajya Sabha member, are reported to record that at least ten people were treated at Delhi government hospitals for pellet or projectile injuries on 20 July 2026: nine at Lady Hardinge Medical College, recorded in the reply as 'pellet/projectile' injuries, and one at Safdarjung Hospital.

sources.originates_from: Right to Information replies obtained by Saket Gokhale from Lady Hardinge Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, reported 13 August 2026

Right to Information replies obtained by Saket Gokhale from Lady Hardinge Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, reported 13 August 2026
Right to Information replies obtained by Saket Gokhale from Lady Hardinge Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, reported 13 August 2026

notes: Saket Gokhale asked four Delhi hospitals a narrow question and two answered it. The archive credits him by name because attribution is how this project treats work it did not do, and because a document obtained by an identified person under a statute is worth more than an anonymous account. What it establishes: that ten people were treated for injuries the hospitals themselves categorised as pellet or projectile injuries, on that date, at those two hospitals. Hospital records are independent of both the police and the petitioners, which is why this sits at CORROBORATED while the question of what was fired stays DISPUTED at INC-DEL-005. What it does not establish: who or what caused the injuries. 'Pellet/projectile' is a clinical category, not a finding about a weapon or about who fired it. It does not say the police fired anything, and it does not distinguish plastic from metallic. It establishes that people arrived at hospital with those injuries on the day of the police action. At least ten, not ten. AIIMS refused (OVR-DEL-002) and Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital had not replied when this was reported. The number is a floor set by which hospitals chose to answer, and the archive states it as one. Not held: the replies themselves. No outlet reproduces them. Obtaining copies would move this to VERIFIED, and it is one of the few claims here where that is straightforwardly achievable: see OQ-047.

claim: The All India Institute of Medical Sciences is reported to have refused a Right to Information application asking how many people were treated for pellet, shot or projectile injuries after the police action of 20 July 2026, citing section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act 2005 on the ground that disclosure could directly or indirectly lead to the identification or tracing of the individual concerned. The refusal was reported on 20 August 2026. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital had not replied as at 13 August 2026.
notes: A refusal is a record, and this one is dated. Two hospitals answered the same question and one declined it. The ground, exactly as reported: section 8(1)(j), personal information, on the basis that disclosure could lead to identification of the individual concerned. The applicant is reported to have said he asked for a number and not for patient details. The archive does not rule on whether the refusal is sound. That is for an appellate authority. There is a clock on this and it is not ours. A first appeal under section 19(1) lies within thirty days of the refusal. The application is Saket Gokhale's, not this project's, so it does not go in the RTI register, which records only applications this project has filed. It is recorded here because the clock is real and because whether an appeal was filed and what came of it is a fact worth following. See OQ-048. One publication only, so REPORTED. The refusal letter itself is not held and is not reproduced anywhere the archive has found.

claim: An open-source investigation published by Alt News on 4 August 2026, based on geolocated bystander video from several angles, reports at least nine rounds fired from AK-47 rifles at two separate locations in Siwan on 25 July 2026 — eight outside the district commandant's office and one on the Kagzi Mohalla to Naya Bazaar road — together with two separate incidents of pistol fire, and more than one police officer firing towards protesters.
notes: One publication, but not of the usual kind. This is not a report of somebody else's document; it is the outlet's own analysis of video it geolocated, which makes it primary work by a secondary source. The archive cannot check it without the footage, so it stays REPORTED, and REPORTED here means 'we have not verified this', not 'we doubt it'. Why it matters: it is the first account of Siwan that does not come from the State of Bihar. Everything else this archive holds about that day is the State describing its own conduct. What it conflicts with: the State's affidavit figure of four AK-47 rounds at JP Chowk. Nine is not four, and the district commandant's office is not JP Chowk. Both cannot be complete. The conflict is recorded at INC-SIW-003, not resolved here. On the named constable: the article identifies in one video the constable the State named and suspended. This archive named him because the State did; it does not add anything to that on the strength of a video it has not seen. What would settle it: the armoury issue and return register for the units deployed at Siwan on 25 July, and any ballistics or forensic report. See OQ-052.

claim: How many rounds were fired by police at Siwan on 25 July 2026, from how many weapons, and at how many locations.

sources.originates_from: State of Bihar affidavit to the Supreme Court, reported 18 August 2026
PUCL Bihar public hearing and fact-finding panel, Patna, 22 August 2026

notes: The state says four ak-47 rounds at one place. An open-source investigation says at least nine at two places, neither of them the place the State names, plus two separate pistol incidents. A civil liberties body's public hearing records firing on students without warning and AK-47 use, but gives no count. A member of Parliament is reported to have denied that AK-47s were used at all. The archive does not split the difference. Averaging four and nine would produce a number nobody has claimed and no document supports. What is not disputed, and is recorded separately at INC-SIW-001: that police discharged firearms at a student protest that day. Everyone accepts that, including the State, which is why it is established while the count is not. The accounts differ in kind, not only in number: four rounds from one trapped constable, or nine from more than one officer at two locations. Armoury records would settle it: see OQ-052.

claim: A public hearing convened by the Bihar unit of the People's Union for Civil Liberties at the IMA Hall, Gandhi Maidan, Patna, on 22 August 2026 heard 19 people who said they were assaulted by police during the student protests of 21 to 27 July 2026. The four-member panel was Basant Chaudhary, senior advocate of the Patna High Court; Sudha Varghese, social worker; Arshad Ajman, social activist; and Pranav Chaudhary, formerly of The Times of India, Patna. The panel is reported to have found lathi charges directed at students including blows aimed at women's genitals, firing on students without warning, custodial torture, and detention beyond 24 hours without production before a magistrate, at Patna, Siwan and Sitamarhi. Its demands include an independent investigation, withdrawal of 64 FIRs and compensation for those shot.

sources.originates_from: PUCL Bihar public hearing and fact-finding panel, Patna, 22 August 2026
PUCL Bihar public hearing and fact-finding panel, Patna, 22 August 2026
PUCL Bihar public hearing and fact-finding panel, Patna, 22 August 2026

notes: What is established here is that the hearing happened and what it found — not that the findings are true. A fact-finding panel is not a court and its conclusions are not evidence of the events; they are the considered account of named people who heard witnesses. The archive records them as that, with the panel named so a reader can weigh it. This is the first account of Bihar that is not the State's. Until now the record for Bihar was almost entirely the government describing itself. Three things it adds that nothing else here had: Sitamarhi, where police are said to have entered a welfare hostel on the evening of 21 July and beaten students, a place and date this archive did not hold; the figure of 64 FIRs; and the reported detention of two PUCL lawyers assisting detained protesters, who are said to have been charged and paraded handcuffed. Sitamarhi is not yet its own incident. Siwan was opened as a separate incident because a State affidavit put it beyond doubt. Sitamarhi rests on one panel's account, and opening an incident on that alone would be a lower standard than the one applied to Siwan. It is recorded here and will be opened when a second, independent account or a document supports it. See OQ-050. The report itself is not held: what the archive has is three outlets' accounts of it. See OQ-049.

claim: An advisory on handling protests, reported as framed by central agencies, has been circulated to Delhi Police personnel across all 15 districts and the Railway and Metro units following the Jantar Mantar police action. It is reported to instruct personnel to stay calm before protesters' cameras, not to argue or engage, to avoid touching women protesters and to leave such situations to women officers, and to assist anyone who faints or is injured.
notes: Read what this advisory is about, and then read what it is not about. As reported, it concerns how officers appear on camera: composure, tone, not being filmed losing one's temper. 'Your angry face is their content' is the line every outlet has quoted. Nothing in any account of it addresses crowd-control weapons, when force may be used, who may authorise it, or what happened on 20 July. The archive draws no conclusion from that absence, because the archive has not read the document and an advisory on conduct is not the place a weapons authority would necessarily sit. What it does record is that this is the only instruction to Delhi Police personnel reported to have issued since 20 July, and that as reported it is about presentation. It is a written instruction to a police force about handling protests, issued by an identifiable authority on an identifiable date. If such an advisory can be circulated to 15 districts, so could an instruction on the use of force, which sharpens the question of whether one governed 20 July. See OQ-053.

claim: On 24 August 2026 the Chief Justice of India is reported to have said that the Court's order of 18 August already requires the High Powered Enquiry Committee to examine allegations of sexual assault, harassment and violence against women protesters as a priority, and to have directed an interim report on those allegations at the earliest. The Court declined to take suo motu cognisance of the allegations, sought by senior counsel Shobha Gupta, and is reported to have said the committee will work under the Court's supervision. A separate plea challenging the composition of the committee is reported to be before the Court.
notes: Two things happened and they are easy to conflate. The Court declined to open a suo motu proceeding on the sexual assault allegations, and the Court said those allegations are already inside the committee's mandate and must be reported on first. A headline can make either of those the story. The archive records both in the same sentence for that reason. What this archive has not recorded and will not until it is sourced: what happened to any woman at Jantar Mantar. The allegations are before a committee and this archive holds no account, no complaint and no medical record. Their existence as allegations is recorded because a court has directed an inquiry into them; nothing about their content is. The challenge to the committee's composition is noted because if it succeeds the committee at PROC-SC-006 changes, and this archive should not be describing a body that has been reconstituted. No order on that challenge is held.

claim: The Union Home Secretary ordered the suspension of mobile internet services, all technologies, within a 1.5 kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, from 16:00 to 24:00 hours on 23 July 2026. The order was addressed to the Commissioner of Delhi Police and made under section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act 2023 read with rule 2(1)(b) and rule 3(1) of the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules 2024. Its stated ground is “in the interest of public order and for preventing incitement to the commission of any offence”.
notes: This is the first record in this archive of an identified authority giving an identified written order affecting one of these incidents. Everything else here concerns force whose author is unknown. Here the office is named in the reporting, the recipient is named, the legal power is cited, the window is fixed to the hour and the ground is quoted. What is established is that the order exists and what it says, on the strength of outlets reproducing its text. What is NOT established, and is deliberately not written above: the name of the officer who signed it, whether it was placed before the Review Committee under rule 3(2) within five days, and whether any of it was ever published. The archive does not hold the order. It holds reports of it. That is the whole point of FQ-014: an order whose text is quoted in the newspapers and absent from every official website is exactly the document this project exists to ask for. Note also what this is not. A communications suspension is not use of force and is not evidence of any. It is recorded because it is a coercive exercise of state power at the same place and time, with an author this archive can name, and because the contrast is the finding: the state's internet order is traceable to a desk and its lathi charge is not.

claim: As at 20 July 2026 no copy of any order suspending telecommunications in Central Delhi had been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police, according to the Internet Freedom Foundation.
notes: IFF's statement of 20 July 2026 says in terms: “At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police.” And: “An unpublished order is an unaccountable order.” The claim is confined to what IFF observed on the day it wrote. This archive has not itself searched every official gazette and portal for the period, and so records this as REPORTED rather than as an established absence. An absence is the hardest thing to prove and the easiest to assert. See OQ-054. Why it matters legally rather than rhetorically: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637 requires suspension orders to be published so they can be challenged. See PREC-SHUT-001.

claim: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637 requires orders suspending telecommunications to be made public, so that they can be challenged, and requires periodic review. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules 2024 provide the review mechanism.
notes: Cited by the Internet Freedom Foundation in its statement of 20 July 2026 alongside the Indian Telegraph Act 1885, the Telecommunications Act 2023 and Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g). Recorded as REPORTED and not VERIFIED because this archive has not fetched the judgment text itself, only IFF's citation of it. The proposition is well known and that is not a reason to record it as established: the rule in this archive is that a claim carries the state of the evidence actually held for it. Fetching the judgment from an authoritative reporter would move it to VERIFIED and is the cheapest upgrade available here. See FQ-015.

claim: By an order reported dated 10 September 2026, a three-judge bench of the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana declined to reconstitute the High Powered Enquiry Committee; directed that a separate online portal be created through which vulnerable witnesses may confidentially submit statements, documents and other evidence; directed the committee to protect the identity and participation of such witnesses; appointed Senior Advocate Monika Gusain and Advocate-on-Record C. Solomon as amici curiae to act as independent intermediaries; and directed the committee to appoint a member secretary for secretarial and logistical support.
notes: This closes a thread the archive left open twice. PROC-SC-006 recorded that the Court listed the matter for 10 September 2026; PROC-SC-010 recorded that a plea challenging the committee's composition was before the Court. This is what happened to both. The refusal is reported on the ground that “there was no basis for changing the panel merely on the strength of preconceived assumptions”. The confidential portal is the part that bears on this archive's own users. Somebody who was assaulted by police and is also named in an FIR has an obvious reason not to depose through ordinary channels. Whether the portal now exists, and at what address, is NOT established: see OQ-054. This archive will not direct anyone to a portal it has not confirmed. Recorded as REPORTED, not CORROBORATED, on a deliberate reading of this archive's own rule. Three outlets carry it, but they are three accounts of one order, and the order is not held. Where the underlying document is a single court order, multiple outlets are multiple reports of one thing, not independent knowledge. The upgrade is the order copy from the Supreme Court's own site: see FQ-014. Amended 23 September 2026 to name the full bench and both amici, and to record the member-secretary direction, all of which the first version of this record left out. The order is dated 10 September and was reported on 16 September; the archive had the order date right and that was worth re-checking, because it was inferred from the listing date at PROC-SC-006 before any source confirmed it.

claim: Accounts of the PUCL Bihar public hearing of 22 August 2026 disagree on how many people deposed and on one panel member's name. INC-BIH-005 records 19 deponents and names the panel as Basant Chaudhary, Sudha Varghese, Arshad Ajman and Pranav Chaudhary. A report published on BiharWatch on 23 August 2026 records 16 oral testimonies and one video testimony, and gives the name as Ajmal Ashraf. The same report enumerates thirteen types of case the panel says it documented.
notes: Recorded rather than resolved, and INC-BIH-005 is left exactly as it stands. Averaging the counts, or quietly adopting whichever was read most recently, would destroy the only useful thing here: that two accounts of one afternoon disagree about a countable fact. Little turns on whether it was 16, 17 or 19 people. What turns on it is that this archive holds no copy of the panel's own report, so every figure it carries about that hearing is an outlet's account of it. OQ-049 already asks for the report. This record is the concrete reason that question is worth answering, and the name disagreement is the sharper half: two of the sources cannot both have the panel right. The thirteen types, as the BiharWatch report lists them: brutal lathi charge injuring students and youth; firing on students and youth resulting in some injuries; using a lethal firearm, an AK-47, on students and youth; custodial torture; illegal detention without production before a magistrate; families not informed of detainees' whereabouts; detainees denied access to family; judicial custody without being informed of the charges; judicial custody without access to a lawyer; destruction of evidence, such as seizing mobile phones; raiding the homes of students and activists without search warrants; obstructing advocates on record and filing unsubstantiated charges against lawyers; and releasing photographs and videos of protesters to the media. These are the panel's characterisations of what it heard from witnesses. They are not findings of this archive, and a fact-finding panel is not a court. The hearing is recorded as held at the IMA Hall, Gandhi Maidan, Patna, on 22 August 2026, which both accounts agree on.

claim: By an interim order reported dated 28 July 2026, the Supreme Court directed that no coercive action be taken against the student protesters save those with criminal antecedents, directed the release of detained minors, directed police to preserve CCTV footage, drone recordings and call logs, restrained publication of protesters' personal data, and recorded a prima facie case for an independent inquiry.
notes: The preservation direction is the part that bears directly on this archive. It is a court order, given eight days after the Delhi incident, to keep the exact categories of record the preservation letters here ask offices to keep: CCTV, drone footage and call logs. An office that destroys any of them on an ordinary retention cycle is now destroying material a court directed it to preserve, which is a different thing to allege and a different thing to ask about. Note also what it does not cover: a deployment order, a wireless log, an armoury issue register. Those still rest on the letters. Recorded as REPORTED rather than CORROBORATED: two outlets carry it, and they are two accounts of one order this archive does not hold.

claim: By an order reported dated 3 August 2026, the Supreme Court clarified that 'criminal antecedents' in its order of 28 July 2026 refers only to persons accused of grave and heinous offences, and held that the NCT of Delhi and the State governments are at liberty to close or withdraw the criminal cases in accordance with law.
notes: A clarification issued because the 28 July carve-out was being read widely. That is worth recording as a fact about how an order of this kind travels: an exception written for people with criminal antecedents was applied to people with any antecedents until the Court said otherwise. The second half matters for the state records: it puts the decision to withdraw back on each state, which is why the withdrawals that follow are executive notifications rather than judicial ones, and an executive notification has an author and a file.

claim: By an order reported dated 1 September 2026 in Yashovardhan Azad and Others v. Union of India and Others and connected matters, a bench of the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana, exercising the power under Article 142 of the Constitution, directed that First Information Reports registered anywhere in India over the student protests held between 20 and 25 July 2026 shall not be pursued or investigated and shall be treated as closed, and that no State or Union Territory shall register a fresh FIR in relation to those incidents, save that Delhi Police may pursue one fresh FIR concerning 2,873 persons said to have serious criminal antecedents.
notes: The single largest legal event on this record and the archive held nothing on it. Applications had been moved by the Centre for Delhi Police and by Bihar, West Bengal, Maharashtra and Assam. The order is reported to be expressly confined to the peculiar facts and not to be treated as a precedent, which is the usual form of an Article 142 direction and should be quoted that way if it is quoted. Two consequences for this archive. First, the FIR records held here for Mumbai, Kochi, Kolkata, Assam and Bihar describe cases that are now closed, and the records say so rather than being deleted: a case that was registered and then closed is a fact about a police force, and removing it would erase the thing worth knowing. Second, the carve-out survives everything else in the order, so the one criminal file still live out of the whole country is the one built on a facial recognition list. See INC-DEL-008 and INC-DEL-009.

claim: Delhi Police stated in an affidavit dated 17 August 2026 before the Supreme Court that its Facial Recognition System identified 2,873 persons with criminal antecedents at the Jantar Mantar protest site between 20 and 26 July 2026, of which 2,402 matches came through Crime Kundli, the force's own biometric database, and 471 through other police records; the deployment is reported to have been run from a Mobile Command and Control Vehicle and a vendor-built van named Ikshana carrying eight fixed cameras and running live CCTV feeds through matching software.
notes: This answers a question this archive had recorded as disputed and could not settle, and it answers it out of the force's own affidavit rather than out of a petitioner's case. PROC-SC-003 asks whether the facial recognition was confined to persons with existing criminal records, as Delhi Police asserted, or ran on the crowd. To return 2,873 matches against a criminal database, a system must first capture and compare the faces it is matching, which is every face it sees. Being confined to persons with criminal records describes what the system was asked to look for, not whom it looked at, and the two have been used interchangeably. The archive does not hold the affidavit: FQ-017 is the copy from the Supreme Court's record. Recorded as REPORTED.

claim: An Indian Express investigation published on 4 September 2026 took the 205 persons on the Delhi Police facial recognition list facing the gravest charges (reported as 101 accused of murder, 61 of rape, six under the POCSO Act and 37 of the 62 accused of attempt to murder) and checked them against police, prison and court records; at least 25 of that sample, one in eight, were in judicial custody in Tihar, Mandoli or Rohini jail on the day the software placed them at Jantar Mantar. Three were identified on 24 July, twenty-one on 25 July and one on 26 July, each with a timestamp. Delhi Police is reported to have said that verification of all 2,873 identifications was pending and that no action would rest on a facial recognition result alone.
notes: A measured error rate in a live police identification system, obtained by the cheapest possible method: comparing one government list against another government list. It is one in eight of a sample chosen for the gravity of the charge rather than at random, so it is not an estimate of the error rate across all 2,873 and should not be quoted as one. What it does establish is that the list was published to a court without that comparison having been made, because the comparison takes custody records that the police and the prisons both already hold. The force's own answer, that verification is pending and no action rests on a match alone, is the admission that matters: the list went to the Supreme Court, and became the basis of the one FIR the Court left standing, before anyone checked it. Credited to The Indian Express; this archive did not do this work and holds neither the list nor the affidavit. The outlets cited below are accounts of one investigation, which is why this is REPORTED.

claim: A nineteen-year-old undergraduate student from Najafgarh, named in the reporting, is reported to have lost vision in his right eye after fragments struck the eye during the police action of 20 July 2026, perforating the cornea; a second operation on 31 July 2026 inserted a lens and vision had not returned; not all fragments were removed.

This is the injury itself, with a date, a procedure and an outcome. It does not establish what was fired: a perforating fragment injury is consistent with more than one munition, and INC-DEL-005 stays disputed. It is the reason the question is worth the work. He is named in every source cited and has spoken publicly under his own name; this archive still does not reproduce the name, on the same rule applied to the complainant at PROC-DEL-003, because a record that outlives the news cycle should not be the thing that keeps a medical fact about a private person searchable. claim: Mumbai Police registered 13 First Information Reports between 18 and 22 July 2026 against more than 400 people for taking part in protests over the NEET examination without police permission, at Shivaji Park, Chaityabhoomi, Chembur and Shiv Sena Bhavan, on charges reported as unlawful assembly, disobedience of an order duly promulgated by a public servant and wrongful restraint; those named were served notices and released, the offences being bailable and carrying a maximum of two years.
notes: This closes INC-MAH-001 and PUB-MAH-001, which have read UNKNOWN since 15 August, and it closes them with an answer nobody was looking for. The archive held open a Maharashtra shell on the strength of a Supreme Court petition saying disturbances had spread there, and went looking for a lathi charge. What is on the record instead is thirteen FIRs against four hundred people for assembling without permission. No use of force in Maharashtra is established here and none is alleged in these sources. That distinction is the finding and the record keeps it: the shell is filled with what happened, not with what the archive expected. It also puts Maharashtra in the same class as Kochi, Kolkata and Assam rather than in the same class as Patna, and that class is the one where a document with an author exists, because a refusal of permission and an FIR are both written by somebody.

claim: Ernakulam Town South police registered a case on its own motion against 101 people, the musician Hirandas Murali, who performs as Vedan, his manager Vignesh G. Pillai, and 99 others, over a solidarity gathering held near Central Park, Panampilly Nagar, Kochi at about 5 pm on Wednesday 22 July 2026 in support of the student protests in Delhi, under sections 190, 223 and 285 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. The First Information Report is reported to state that the organisers went ahead after being served a notice refusing permission.
notes: Kerala was not on this archive before today. It is here for one reason, and it is the reason the whole site exists: the FIR says a notice refusing permission was served. That notice is a written order. It has a date, a signatory, an office and a file, and unlike a lathi charge it cannot have happened without leaving one. The question this archive asks of a baton is unanswerable because a baton leaves no paper; asked of a refusal of permission it is answerable by an RTI application to a named police station. No use of force is established at Kochi and none is alleged in these sources. The three sections carry the archive's standing caution on statute: they are quoted as the reports give them and have not been checked against the current text by anyone who practises.

claim: Seven cases were registered in Kolkata over the student protests, with about 70 persons identified, reported on 28 July 2026, on which date the West Bengal government's decision on withdrawal was reported as still pending. The state is reported to have said there would be no coercive action in cases registered up to 6 pm on 26 July 2026.
notes: Recorded as evidence and NOT opened as an incident shell. There is no located place, no date of any police action and no account of force: what is established is that seven files exist and about seventy people are named in them. That is not enough to open a record called an incident, and the archive has refused on this ground before: Sitamarhi was left unopened on a single account for the same reason. If the location and date of a Kolkata action are established, or the seven case numbers obtained, this becomes a shell. Until then it is a fact about a police force's paperwork, which is worth holding and is not the same thing.

claim: Five cases were registered in Assam over the student protests and 13 people arrested, reported on 28 July 2026; the Assam government issued a notification stating that the process of withdrawing the registered cases would be initiated as per law promptly, and that those arrested would be released.
notes: Recorded as evidence and NOT opened as an incident shell, on the same reasoning as INC-WB-001: no place, no date, no account of force. What makes it worth holding is the notification. A state withdrawing criminal cases does it by a written instrument that names an office and carries a date, and it is obtainable by RTI from the Assam Home Department in a way that a decision to charge never is. Bihar issued one on the same day and the two were shown to the CJP delegation together. Note the units before comparing states: Bihar is reported at 694 detained and 355 booked, Assam at 13 arrested and 5 cases, Mumbai at 400 booked and 13 FIRs, Kolkata at about 70 in 7 cases. People booked, people arrested, people detained and cases registered are four different counts and the reporting moves between them.

claim: 694 people are reported to have been detained in Bihar over the student protests and 355 booked; the Bihar Home Department issued a notification, reported on 28 July 2026, withdrawing the cases and stating that no adverse legal action shall be taken against protesters in respect of matters before 6 pm on 26 July 2026, with those in custody to be released.
notes: The largest set of figures the archive holds for Bihar, and the first that comes from the state rather than from a fact-finding panel. It does not contradict the 64 FIRs the PUCL hearing reported at INC-BIH-005: an FIR can name many people, so 355 booked in an unstated number of files and 64 FIRs are not two answers to one question. The cut-off is the part to keep. A withdrawal expressed as a time on a date, 6 pm on 26 July, is drawn from a file, and the file is obtainable from the Bihar Home Department. It is also the same cut-off West Bengal is reported to have used, which is worth knowing when asking either state where the line came from.

claim: On Friday 2 October 2026 Delhi Police detained several hundred people who were trying to reach Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. The counts differ by source and the archive holds no official statement of any of them. Al Jazeera reports over 500 by about 3 pm. Deccan Chronicle reports over 500, with one official first giving 150 and another about 500. The Week and Outlook report over 700, Outlook attributing the figure to police officials. ThePrint, in its report of 3 October, says approximately 1,000 people were detained on the Friday. Hindustan Times, as carried by Outlook, is reported to give about 1,000 across Delhi: nearly 750 near Jantar Mantar and about 400 elsewhere, with around 200 held under house arrest beforehand. Reuters describes batches of student protesters put onto buses and taken away. Those detained are reported to include opposition political leaders and members of the student organisations AISA, SFI and NSUI.
notes: The figures differ but may not conflict: 500 by mid-afternoon, 700 and about 1,000 by the end of the day are consistent with each other, and most sources do not say when each count was taken. The components reported for the Hindustan Times figure do not sum to 1,000 as they are summarised, which is a reason to read the original before quoting it. The archive records every figure and does not choose. Detention under a prohibitory order is not a finding of force, and this record makes none. Outlook reports Delhi Police, the Rapid Action Force and the CRPF at the site, and quotes a Delhi Police officer putting the deployment at more than 1,000 personnel; its later report, citing Hindustan Times, says more than 5,000. Al Jazeera reports at least 11 metro stations closed; Deccan Chronicle says 12. Al Jazeera takes its figures from Reuters and The Times of India, so it is not independent of them; the others are separate reports.

claim: Delhi Police refused permission for the protest planned at Jantar Mantar on 2 October 2026. claim: IBTimes India reports that Delhi Police personnel at the Jantar Mantar protests did not wear name tags, that junior personnel were allowed to remove them while most IPS officers kept theirs, and that officials gave the reason as preventing individual officers being identified and targeted on social media after the protest of 20 July, with junior personnel assured that no action would follow if they acted within the law.
notes: One outlet. Hindustan Times and The Times of India headlines in the 5 October sweep carry the same story and were not retrieved. The record matters to this archive for a plain reason: an officer who cannot be identified cannot be asked who gave an order, and the explanation offered concerns harassment of officers and their families, which is a real harm and is recorded as the police's stated reason and not as the archive's view.

claim: PTI and Deccan Chronicle report that three women journalists alleged sexual harassment by police personnel during the Jantar Mantar protest of 3 October 2026, that no FIR was registered when they went to a police station, and that Delhi Police transferred the complaints to the Crime Branch for what an unnamed New Delhi district officer called a fair and impartial enquiry. notes: The complainants are not named here. PTI reports that an Assistant Commissioner of Police is named in the complaint and could not be reached for comment; the officer is not named in this record, on the rule that an unproven allegation does not put a name in the archive.
